# Learning from Experiments {#sec-experiments}

*Driving question: **Did it work?***

Randomized experiments are the most credible way to learn what an action *causes* (@sec-randomization). But running an experiment is only half of the job: the result comes from a sample, and every sample carries random error (@sec-uncertainty). This chapter is about the second half — how to read the result of an experiment. After working through this chapter you will be able to:

- Explain the logic of a statistical test: comparing the observed difference with the differences that chance alone would produce
- Run and interpret a *t*-test for the difference between two groups — and read every line of its output
- Choose the right *t*-test for the design: the Welch test for **between-subjects** data, the paired test for **within-subjects** data
- Distinguish **statistical significance** from **practical relevance**, and quantify the size of an effect
- Compare **shares** (e.g., conversion rates) between groups
- Explain type I and type II errors and **statistical power** — and determine the sample size an experiment needs *before* running it
- Choose an appropriate test for other designs: more than two groups and skewed data
- Use *p*-values responsibly — and recognize practices that make them meaningless

The chapter builds on the Smart Mix A/B test from @sec-unc-abtest. The formulas are kept to a minimum: we compute a standard error once, by hand, to see what a test does — afterwards, R does the arithmetic, and we concentrate on the interpretation.

## Back to the A/B test {#sec-exp-abtest}

Recall the situation: a streaming service tested its new *Smart Mix* feature on 400 randomly selected users. The 200 users with Smart Mix listened `r round(diff(rev(tapply(ab_data()$hours, ab_data()$group, mean))), 1)` hours more on average in four weeks than the 200 users without it (@fig-ab-recap).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ab-recap
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "The Smart Mix A/B test as Chapter 3 left it: group means with their 95% confidence intervals (simulated data; see @sec-unc-abtest)."
fig_ab_bars(ci = TRUE)
```

In @sec-unc-abtest, we ran a *t*-test and postponed its interpretation. Here is the output again:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(31)
ab_test <- tibble(
  group = factor(rep(c("Control", "Smart Mix"), each = 200), levels = c("Smart Mix", "Control")),
  hours = c(rgamma(200, shape = 2, scale = 10), rgamma(200, shape = 2, scale = 11.5))
)

t.test(hours ~ group, data = ab_test)
```

The product team wants answers to three questions, and this chapter takes them in turn:

1.  **Could the difference be chance?** Even if Smart Mix did nothing, two random groups of 200 users would never have exactly the same mean. Is 3.2 hours more than chance would typically produce? (@sec-exp-difference and @sec-exp-testing)
2.  **How large is the effect — and does it matter?** A "real" effect can still be too small to be worth the rollout. (@sec-exp-effect)
3.  **Was the experiment large enough?** Would a larger experiment have given a clearer answer — and how large should the next one be? (@sec-exp-power)

## The difference between two means {#sec-exp-difference}

### Signal and noise

The key to the first question is an idea you already know from @sec-uncertainty: any number computed from a sample varies from sample to sample. This also holds for the *difference* between two group means. If we could repeat the Smart Mix experiment many times — each time with 400 new users, randomly split — we would get a slightly different difference every time. The distribution of these differences is the **sampling distribution of the difference**, and it has the same three properties as the sampling distribution of a mean:

1.  It is **centered on the true difference** in the population — the true effect of Smart Mix.
2.  It is **approximately normal** — thanks to the central limit theorem, even though listening times are skewed.
3.  Its width is the **standard error of the difference**, which combines the uncertainty of both group means:

$$
SE_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}
$$

For Smart Mix: $\sqrt{16.2^2 / 200 + 13.7^2 / 200}$ = 1.50 hours. Differences of about ± 1.5 hours are therefore the "typical wobble" we must expect from random sampling alone; differences of about ± 3 hours (two standard errors) are rare, but possible.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Under the hood: why the variances add"}
The standard error of one mean is $s / \sqrt{n}$; its square, $s^2 / n$, is the *variance* of the sample mean. For two **independent** quantities, the **variance sum law** states that the variance of their difference is the sum of their variances: $\text{Var}(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) = s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2$ — the minus sign vanishes because subtracting an uncertain number adds uncertainty just as adding one does. Taking the square root gives the formula above. Uncertainties therefore combine like the sides of a right triangle, not end to end: two standard errors of 1.1 and 1.0 hours give 1.5, not 2.1, because random errors in the two groups partly cancel. The law has one condition — independence. When the two measurements belong to the same person, as in the paired design of @sec-exp-other, they are correlated, the covariance is subtracted, and the standard error of the difference becomes *smaller*: $\text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) - 2\,\text{Cov}(X, Y)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it: one experiment, one difference" icon="false"}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof d1_runs = Inputs.button(
  [["Run 1 experiment", v => v + 1], ["Run 100 experiments", v => v + 100], ["Reset", v => 1]],
  {value: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof d1_n = Inputs.radio([50, 200, 800], {value: 200, label: "Users per group",
  format: d => d.toLocaleString("en")})
```
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
d1 = {
  const rng = d3.randomLcg(77);
  const gc = d3.randomGamma.source(rng)(2, 10), gt = d3.randomGamma.source(rng)(2, 11.5);
  const n = d1_n, diffs = [];
  let last = null;
  for (let k = 0; k < d1_runs; k++) {
    const c = Array.from({length: n}, () => gc()), t = Array.from({length: n}, () => gt());
    const mc = d3.mean(c), mt = d3.mean(t);
    diffs.push(mt - mc);
    if (k === d1_runs - 1) last = {c, t, mc, mt};
  }
  const se = Math.sqrt((2 * 10 ** 2) / n + (2 * 11.5 ** 2) / n);
  return {diffs, last, n, se};
}
```

**What to look for.** Every experiment gives a different difference — sometimes 1 hour, sometimes 5, now and then even a negative one, although the true effect is always +3 hours. Run 100 experiments: the differences pile up around the true effect in a bell shape, and their spread matches the standard error. Switch to 50 or 800 users per group and watch the spread change.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof d2_shape = Inputs.select(
  ["Right-skewed (listening hours)", "Symmetric (normal)", "Two groups (casual and heavy listeners)", "Yes/no (upgrade to Premium)"],
  {label: "Outcome"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof d2_n = Inputs.range([2, 300], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "Users per group"})
```
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
d2 = {
  const rng = d3.randomLcg(13);
  const nrm = d3.randomNormal.source(rng), gam = d3.randomGamma.source(rng);
  let gc, gt, binary = false;
  if (d2_shape.startsWith("Right")) { const a = gam(2, 10), b = gam(2, 11.5); gc = () => a(); gt = () => b(); }
  else if (d2_shape.startsWith("Symmetric")) { const a = nrm(20, 14), b = nrm(23, 14); gc = () => a(); gt = () => b(); }
  else if (d2_shape.startsWith("Two")) {
    const lo = nrm(10, 3), hi = nrm(40, 6);
    gc = () => rng() < 0.4 ? hi() : lo(); gt = () => rng() < 0.5 ? hi() : lo();
  } else { binary = true; gc = () => rng() < 0.05 ? 1 : 0; gt = () => rng() < 0.065 ? 1 : 0; }
  const popC = Float64Array.from({length: 20000}, gc), popT = Float64Array.from({length: 20000}, gt);
  const k = binary ? 100 : 1;                         // shares in percentage points
  const mu = k * (d3.mean(popT) - d3.mean(popC));
  const n = d2_n, reps = 3000;
  const se = k * Math.sqrt(d3.variance(popC) / n + d3.variance(popT) / n);
  const diffs = Float64Array.from({length: reps}, () => {
    let a = 0, b = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { a += gc(); b += gt(); }
    return k * (b - a) / n;
  });
  const pmin = Math.min(d3.min(popC), d3.min(popT)), pmax = Math.max(d3.max(popC), d3.max(popT));
  const pthr = binary ? [-0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 1.25] : d3.range(pmin, pmax + (pmax - pmin) / 40, (pmax - pmin) / 40);
  const lo = d3.min(diffs), hi = d3.max(diffs);
  const bw = binary ? Math.max(100 / n, (hi - lo) / 40) : (hi - lo) / 40;
  const curve = d3.range(lo, hi, (hi - lo) / 200).map(x => ({x, y: reps * bw * Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / se) ** 2) / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))}));
  return {popC, popT, pthr, diffs, mu, se, lo, hi, bw, curve, binary};
}
```

```{ojs}

{
  const left = Plot.plot({
    width: 380, height: 250, marginLeft: 55,
    x: {label: d2.binary ? "Upgraded (0 = no, 1 = yes)" : "Value of the outcome"},
    y: {label: "Users", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(d2.popC, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: d2.pthr, fill: "#d99a2b", fillOpacity: 0.55})),
      Plot.rectY(d2.popT, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: d2.pthr, fill: "#0f5da8", fillOpacity: 0.45}))
    ]
  });
  const right = Plot.plot({
    width: 380, height: 250, marginLeft: 55,
    x: {label: d2.binary ? "Difference in shares, percentage points (treatment − control)" : "Difference in means (treatment − control)"},
    y: {label: "Experiments", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rectY(d2.diffs, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: d3.range(d2.lo, d2.hi + d2.bw, d2.bw), fill: "#0f5da8"})),
      Plot.line(d2.curve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#d99a2b", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]
  });
  return html`<div style="display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:1em;">
    <div><b>The two populations</b>${left}</div>
    <div><b>Differences in 3,000 experiments with ${d2_n} users per group</b>${right}</div></div>`;
}
```

**What to look for.** With only a handful of users per group, the differences inherit the shape of the data — skewed, lumpy, or (for yes/no outcomes) jumping in coarse steps. As the groups grow, the differences become bell-shaped for every type of outcome, as the central limit theorem predicts. Yes/no outcomes with rare successes need the largest groups — which is why conversion tests need so many users (@sec-exp-power).
:::

This is the only standard error we compute by hand in this chapter. Every test that follows works on the same principle: it compares the **signal** (the observed difference) with the **noise** (the standard error — the differences chance alone would produce).

### A world in which Smart Mix does nothing

To judge whether 3.2 hours is a lot, imagine a world in which Smart Mix has *no effect at all*: all users come from the same population, and any difference between the groups is pure chance. @fig-null-world simulates 10,000 A/B tests in this world.

```{r}
#| label: fig-null-world
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| fig-cap: "The sampling distribution of the difference if Smart Mix has no effect: 10,000 simulated A/B tests with 200 users per group. Differences at least as large as the observed one (in either direction) are shown in orange."
fig_null_world()
```

In this no-effect world, the differences scatter around zero in a bell shape, as the central limit theorem predicts. A difference as large as the one we observed — 3.2 hours or more, in either direction — occurs in only about 3.6% of the simulated tests. So either Smart Mix has an effect, or the team observed a fairly rare accident. This comparison is exactly what a statistical test formalizes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it: how surprising is the observed difference?" icon="false"}

The chart shows 2,000 simulated A/B tests **in a world in which Smart Mix has no effect**. The orange bars mark the tests whose difference is at least as large as the observed one. Change the **sample size per group** and the **observed difference**: when is a difference of 3.2 hours surprising — and when is it not?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function pnorm(x) {
  // standard normal distribution function (Abramowitz & Stegun 26.2.17)
  const t = 1 / (1 + 0.2316419 * Math.abs(x));
  const d = 0.3989422804 * Math.exp(-x * x / 2);
  const p = d * t * (0.319381530 + t * (-0.356563782 + t * (1.781477937 + t * (-1.821255978 + t * 1.330274429))));
  return x > 0 ? 1 - p : p;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function qnorm(p) {
  // inverse of the standard normal distribution (Acklam's algorithm)
  const a = [-3.969683028665376e+01, 2.209460984245205e+02, -2.759285104469687e+02, 1.383577518672690e+02, -3.066479806614716e+01, 2.506628277459239e+00];
  const b = [-5.447609879822406e+01, 1.615858368580409e+02, -1.556989798598866e+02, 6.680131188771972e+01, -1.328068155288572e+01];
  const c = [-7.784894002430293e-03, -3.223964580411365e-01, -2.400758277161838e+00, -2.549732539343734e+00, 4.374664141464968e+00, 2.938163982698783e+00];
  const d = [7.784695709041462e-03, 3.224671290700398e-01, 2.445134137142996e+00, 3.754408661907416e+00];
  const pl = 0.02425, ph = 1 - pl;
  let q, r;
  if (p < pl) { q = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(p));
    return (((((c[0]*q+c[1])*q+c[2])*q+c[3])*q+c[4])*q+c[5]) / ((((d[0]*q+d[1])*q+d[2])*q+d[3])*q+1); }
  if (p <= ph) { q = p - 0.5; r = q * q;
    return (((((a[0]*r+a[1])*r+a[2])*r+a[3])*r+a[4])*r+a[5])*q / (((((b[0]*r+b[1])*r+b[2])*r+b[3])*r+b[4])*r+1); }
  q = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(1 - p));
  return -(((((c[0]*q+c[1])*q+c[2])*q+c[3])*q+c[4])*q+c[5]) / ((((d[0]*q+d[1])*q+d[2])*q+d[3])*q+1);
}
```

```{ojs}

viewof e1_n = Inputs.range([25, 800], {value: 200, step: 1, label: "Users per group", transform: Math.log, invert: Math.exp})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof e1_obs = Inputs.range([0, 8], {value: 3.2, step: 0.1, label: "Observed difference (hours)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
e1 = {
  const rng = d3.randomLcg(11);
  const gam = d3.randomGamma.source(rng)(2, 10.75);
  const n = Math.round(e1_n), reps = 2000;
  const diffs = Array.from({length: reps}, () => {
    let a = 0, b = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { a += gam(); b += gam(); }
    return (a - b) / n;
  });
  const sd = 10.75 * Math.sqrt(2);                 // SD of the gamma(2, 10.75) population
  const se = sd * Math.sqrt(2 / n);
  const share = diffs.filter(d => Math.abs(d) >= e1_obs).length / reps;
  const lim = Math.max(4.5 * se, e1_obs + se);
  const bw = lim / 30;
  const curve = d3.range(-lim, lim, lim / 150).map(x => ({x, y: reps * bw * Math.exp(-0.5 * (x / se) ** 2) / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))}));
  return {diffs, se, share, lim, bw, curve, n};
}
```
